entries.name: Paleo-Indians (Clovis)
climate: end of the last ice age; transition to Holocene
entries.settlement: highly mobile bands following game
trade: obsidian and flint across long distances
entries.beliefs: shamanic; megafauna hunting ritual
entries.fell_by: megafauna extinction, climate shift; dispersed into Archaic cultures
entries.notes: The oldest horizon: any deep-ruin layer in the game can be a Clovis camp.

entries.name: Olmec
entries.region: Gulf Coast lowlands, Veracruz and Tabasco
entries.settlement: regal-ritual centres with earthen platforms amid farmland
entries.beliefs: were-jaguar rain and earth powers; colossal heads were likely rulers
entries.fell_by: unknown; centres emptied by 400 BCE, heartland reused by later peoples
entries.notes: “Olmec” is a Nahuatl nickname meaning “rubber people”; their own name is lost, and their language is unwritten and unidentified.

entries.name: Epi-Olmec (Izapan)
entries.region: Gulf lowlands and Pacific slope, Isthmus of Tehuantepec
entries.settlement: temple mounds tied to coastal trade routes
trade: cacao and crafts between Gulf and Pacific
entries.beliefs: feathered-serpent and toad imagery, ancestor cults
entries.fell_by: superseded by classic states around 200 CE
entries.notes: Its Tuxtla statuette (162 CE) carries one of Mesoamerica's oldest dated inscriptions; the language is undeciphered.

entries.name: Zapotec
entries.settlement: Monte Albán hilltop capital with Danzantes gallery
entries.beliefs: Cocijo, lightning-rain lord; mountain and maize powers; dead housed in tombs under homes
entries.fell_by: never fell statewide; capital shifted to Mitla and Zaachila, conquered by Spanish-Mixtec alliances 1521-26; Zapotec people persist
entries.notes: Monte Albán was one of the first great planned cities in the Americas, deliberately built on a flattened mountain.

entries.name: Mixtec
entries.settlement: small fortified hilltop towns ruled by dynasties
entries.beliefs: persons of the rain; codices record dynastic history and ritual calendar
entries.fell_by: conquest era; lordships subjugated by Spain and its Zapotec allies by the 1520s; Mixtec people persist
entries.notes: Their codices feuded less with facts than with dynasties; “8 Deer Jaguar Claw” is the most retold life in Mesoamerican history.

entries.name: Teotihuacanos
entries.settlement: one gridded metropolis of some 100 000-200 000 with apartment compounds and barrios of outsiders
entries.beliefs: storm and water powers; the Pyramids of Sun and Moon keyed to sacred geography
entries.fell_by: burned and abandoned around 650 CE; cause debated (revolt, invasion, climate, over-extraction)
entries.notes: A multiethnic city, not a nation; its builders left no readable name for themselves, so “Teotihuacan” is the later Nahuatl word for “the place where the gods were made.”

entries.name: Classic Maya
entries.region: Petén highlands and lowlands, Belize, Yucatán, Honduras
entries.settlement: divine kingdoms (ajawlil) of stone capitals in rainforest
trade: quetzal feathers, jade and obsidian around the lowlands
entries.beliefs: divine kingship (k'uhul ajaw); Long Count calendrics; maize-father story; bloodletting
entries.fell_by: classic collapse 800-900 CE (drought, war, overpopulation); kingdoms fell or moved north
entries.notes: Hundreds of city-states, not an empire; model them as rival kingdoms with shared script and calendar.

entries.name: Yucatec Maya
entries.region: Yucatán Peninsula; present in Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche
entries.settlement: walled cities and later haciendas around cenotes
entries.beliefs: ajaw and k'uh; cenotes as water portals; Venus warfare tables
entries.fell_by: conquered in the 1540s; the Caste War (1847-1901) burned the peninsula; Maya people persist strongly
entries.notes: The only Mesoamerican people who actively read their own post-conquest books (Chilam Balam) to relearn their history.

entries.name: Itza Maya
entries.region: Petén, Guatemala; later the whole northern lowlands
entries.settlement: island-and-causeway stronghold at Nojpetén
entries.beliefs: k'uhul ajaw kingship; Chaac rain lord; Venus timing
entries.fell_by: seventeen Spanish assaults over 150 years; Nojpetén fell to Martín de Ursúa in 1697 - the last independent indigenous state in the Americas
entries.notes: The single most defiant entry in the file: unconquered 176 years after the fall of Tenochtitlan.

entries.name: Lacandón
entries.settlement: scattered rainforest hamlets practising milpa rotation
trade: xate and rubber to lumber camps
entries.beliefs: household god pots to major Maya deities; maintain pre-Columbian-style incense rites
entries.fell_by: never conquered as a nation; reduced by disease and forced resettlement, survive in a shrinking remnant forest
entries.notes: Closest living bridge to the Classic Maya: their god pots are actively fed and talked to today.

entries.name: K'iche'
entries.settlement: highland confederations around Utatlán (K'umarcaaj)
entries.beliefs: K'ucumatz and Q'uq'umatz (feathered serpent); Heart of Sky and Earth makers
entries.fell_by: Tecum Uman killed at the Battle of El Pinar (Tecpán) in 1524; capital burned; K'iche' people persist
entries.notes: Authors of the Popol Vuh, the greatest surviving prose of the pre-Columbian world.

entries.name: Kaqchikel
entries.region: Central highlands and Lake Atitlán, Guatemala
entries.settlement: fortified highland cities around Iximché
entries.beliefs: dual creator pair; sea and mountain lords; calendric prayer
entries.fell_by: allied with Cortés 1524, revolted when burdened with forced labour; Iximché burned 1524; Kaqchikel people persist
entries.notes: Switched sides and paid for it: the revolt was crushed city by city by 1530.

entries.name: Mam
entries.settlement: fortified mountain towns (Zaculeu) and terraced valleys
entries.beliefs: Mam grandfather spirit as first earth soul; mountain and ravine cults
entries.fell_by: Zaculeu fell to the Spanish and K'iche' allies in 1525 after a long siege; Mam people persist
entries.notes: “Mam” is a Maya word for grandfather or ancestor; the name says who they think they came from.

entries.name: Mexica (Aztec)
entries.region: Basin of Mexico; empire from Pánuco to Guatemala
entries.settlement: dual island city of Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco; Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan
entries.beliefs: Huitzilopochtli solar war cult; blood and hearts feed the sun; Quetzalcoatl; 52-year fire-drill renewal
entries.fell_by: Cortés, Tlaxcalan allies and smallpox; Tenochtitlan fell 13 August 1521; Nahuatl-speaking people persist
entries.notes: “Aztec” is a later scholarly name (from Aztlán); they called themselves Mexica. Their empire was a tribute ring of reluctant allies, which is why so many joined Cortés.

entries.name: Tlaxcalans
entries.settlement: four confederated altepetl ringed by the Mexica; never conquered
entries.beliefs: Camaxtle fire and hunting deity, close to Mixcoatl
entries.fell_by: never fell to the Mexica; became Spain's favoured allies and kept a measure of autonomy as a colonial republic; Tlaxcalan people persist
entries.notes: “Tlaxcala” is the Nahuatl for “a place abounding in tortillas”; its warriors decided the fall of Tenochtitlan.

entries.name: Cholulans
entries.settlement: plains market town under the Great Pyramid of Tepanapa
trade: luxury goods for the Mexica in
entries.beliefs: Quetzalcoatl cult centre; the largest pyramid ever built on Earth by volume
entries.fell_by: October 1519: Cortés and Tlaxcalans massacred thousands in the great plaza; surviving Cholula persists as a colonial city
entries.notes: The pyramid is 65 m high and broader than Giza's Great Pyramid; a Spanish church now sits on top of it.

entries.name: Toltec
entries.region: Tula, Hidalgo; influence across central Mexico and the Gulf
entries.settlement: fortified acropolis at Tula with Atlantean colonnades
trade: obsidian weaponry and plumbate ware out
entries.beliefs: Quetzalcoatl (the Feathered Serpent) as priest-king; Tula as his home city
entries.fell_by: burned and abandoned around 1150 CE; cause debated (drought, civil war, Chichimec incursion)
entries.notes: More legend than empire: later peoples invoked “Toltec” as a byword for civilized arts the way Europe invokes Rome.

entries.name: Purépecha (Tarascan)
entries.region: Michoacán; the only state never taken by the Mexica
entries.settlement: lake-district capitals, Tzintzuntzan of rounded yácatas
entries.beliefs: Curicaveri, the fire god; sacrifice to him kept the world warm
entries.fell_by: Nuño de Guzmán's campaigns 1529-30; capital taken and population massacred or enslaved; Purépecha people persist
entries.notes: First and foremost metallurgists in Mesoamerica; their bronze outclassed Mexica obsidian and they stayed independent to the end.

entries.name: Totonac
entries.settlement: El Tajín and Cempoala capitals; mound and ballcourt centres
entries.beliefs: storm and lightning gods; ballcourt as cosmic contest
entries.fell_by: allied with Cortés initially, absorbed into New Spain by the 1520s; Totonac people persist
entries.notes: Vanilla was domesticated only here in the world until the 19th century; every vanilla pod in Europe passed through Totonac hands.

entries.name: Huastec (Tenek)
entries.region: Huasteca, northern Veracruz and San Luis Potosí
entries.settlement: autonomous gulf-to-plateau towns, never united into one state
entries.beliefs: closest Maya-speaking cousins to the great Maya temples, living at the northern edge
entries.fell_by: conquest 1521-30s; incorporated into New Spain; Huastec (Tenek) people persist
entries.notes: The northernmost Maya people; their language split off from the rest of Maya so early that Maya and Huastec are barely mutually intelligible.

entries.name: Otomí (Hñähñu)
entries.settlement: market towns between the valleys and the northern frontier
entries.beliefs: Old Otomí rain and fire gods; pulque as divine gift
entries.fell_by: never a single state; absorbed into Mexica tribute then New Spain; Otomí people persist
entries.notes: They lived on both sides of the northern “Chichimec frontier”; Otomí were often the bridge and buffer between the empire and the nomadic north.

entries.name: Matlatzinca
entries.settlement: valley cities conquered in turn by Toltecs, Tepanecs and Mexica
entries.beliefs: rain and lake powers; Nahua-inflected by the late period
entries.fell_by: conquered by Axayacatl around 1474-76; language now survives only around San Francisco Oxtotilpan, Mexico
entries.notes: Name from Nahuatl matlatl, “net” - “net-speakers”; one of the few Mesoamerican languages brought to the edge of extinction by Nahuatl expansion itself.

entries.name: Chichimec
entries.settlement: bands, not states; circular reed and hide camps
trade: salt and feathers out when trading
entries.beliefs: hunter-gatherer shamanism; gods of game and dry country
entries.fell_by: the Chichimeca War (1550-1590) ended armed northern independence; survivors absorbed into northern towns
entries.notes: “Chichimec” is a Nahuatl umbrella for “uncivilized northerners”; the label included many unrelated nations with one in common: they did not farm.

entries.name: Wixárika (Huichol)
entries.region: Sierra Madre Occidental, Nayarit and Jalisco
entries.settlement: dispersed ranchitos and ceremonial centres
entries.beliefs: Sun Father and Maize Goddess; annual peyote pilgrimage to Wirikuta
entries.fell_by: never conquered as a nation; Spanish and Mexican states encroached slowly; Wixárika people persist prominently
entries.notes: Their peyote pilgrimage to the desert of Wirikuta, several hundred kilometres from home, is the most spectacular surviving rite in Mesoamerica.

entries.name: Cora (Nayehri)
entries.settlement: mountain villages with ceremonial centres
entries.beliefs: close cousin of Huichol religion; peyote and sun-father cults, later blended with saints
entries.fell_by: never conquered outright; in the Sierra during the conquest era and early republic; Cora people persist
entries.notes: The 1722-23 Nayarit revolt under an unnamed leader, showed how far from conquest the western Sierra still was two centuries on.

entries.name: Chontal Maya
entries.region: Tabasco and Campeche plains, Gulf Coast trade corridor
entries.settlement: port towns along lagoon systems; Xicalango as a great entrepôt
entries.beliefs: feathered serpent and Venus cults shared with Chichén Itzá and the Mexican highlands
entries.fell_by: absorbed into New Spain in the 1520s; Chontal Maya-speaking communities persist in Tabasco
entries.notes: “Chontal” is what Nahuatl speakers called them - “foreigners”; the name stuck to exceptional merchants in canoes.

entries.name: Zoque
entries.region: Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Chiapas and Tabasco
entries.settlement: ceremonial centres at La Venta adjacency and modern municipio towns
entries.beliefs: jaguar and rain powers; continuation of the Olmec heartland cult
entries.fell_by: never a single state; colonial rule came early; Zoque people persist
entries.notes: Mixe-Zoquean languages are the prime candidate for the Olmec tongue, making the Zoque the nearest thing to Olmec descendants.

entries.name: Pipil (Nawat)
entries.region: El Salvador and adjacent Guatemala and Honduras
entries.settlement: Cuzcatlán, a fortified lagoon city of 40 000, capital of a league of Nahua towns
entries.beliefs: Sun and rain gods carried from central Mexico; burial in round stone graves
entries.fell_by: Pedro de Alvarado took Cuzcatlán in 1524; Pipil revolt crushed 1526-29; Nawat-speaking communities persist, endangered
entries.notes: Right at the southern edge of Mesoamerica; their exquisitely preserved village of Joya de Cerén, buried by volcano around 600 CE, is our best Pompeii.

entries.name: Lenca
entries.settlement: hamlets and mountain towns speaking the Lencan language family
entries.beliefs: Lencan earth and mountain spirits; blended with Catholic saints early
entries.fell_by: conquered piecemeal 1536-37; the resistance leader Lempira died under Spanish siege or treachery in 1538; Lenca people persist
entries.notes: Lempira gives his name to the Honduran currency and is the national symbol of Honduran resistance.

entries.name: Chorotega
subsistence: salted fish from the Gulf of Nicoya
entries.settlement: chiefdoms at Nicoya and Diriamba; open plaza-and-mound towns
entries.beliefs: Nahua-influenced rain and sun cults; syncretized into Catholic feast days
entries.fell_by: Gil González Dávila 1522-23; decimated by slave raids and disease; Chorotega-speaking communities survive in Guanacaste
entries.notes: “Chorotega” is what later Nicarao Nahuas called them; they were the last major northern-Mexican migrant wave to Nicaragua, maybe 700-900 CE.

entries.name: Nicarao
entries.settlement: Nahua-style fortified island towns; Granada precursor of Nahuatl origin
trade: cacao entrepôt between Mayas and southern chiefdoms
entries.beliefs: Mixed Mexican and local cults; consensus that their name gave Nicaragua its name
entries.fell_by: fell to Gil González Dávila in 1522-23 and Alvarado's campaigns 1524; extinct as a distinct group within two generations
entries.notes: “Nicaragua” is almost certainly “Nicarao” plus Spanish -agua; Gil González reportedly interviewed the paramount chief Nicarao in 1522.

entries.name: Nahua peoples
entries.region: Central Mexico; diaspora to Central America
entries.settlement: altepetl - city-states of common lineage and cult
entries.beliefs: Quetzalcoatl, Tezcatlipoca, Xipe Totec, Tlaloc; 52-year calendar round
entries.fell_by: each group met its own end; the collective survives as the largest indigenous language family in Mexico (~2 million speakers)
entries.notes: “Aztec” is one people; “Nahua” is the language-family umbrella - every Nahuatl speaker, from Nayarit to El Salvador, is Nahua.

entries.name: Tlapanec (Me'phaa)
entries.settlement: autonomous hill towns; sometimes subject to the Mexica and Mixtec
entries.beliefs: Me'phaa mountain and thunder spirits; blend of local and Nahua cults
entries.fell_by: never a single state; Mexica tributary, then Spain's; Tlapanec people persist robustly
entries.notes: “Tlapanec” is Nahuatl for “people of the red ochre”; they call themselves Me'phaa. Guerrero hill towns still resist outside classification.

entries.name: Chiapanec
entries.region: Chiapa de Corzo and the Grijalva depression, Chiapas
entries.settlement: fortified Grijalva valley cities (Chiapa proper)
entries.beliefs: Otomanguean-speaking valley cults; sumidero canyon as sacred landscape
entries.fell_by: fell to Alvarado in 1524-25; the language went nearly extinct by the 20th century; Chiapanec identity persists around Chiapa de Corzo
entries.notes: One of the few southern languages on the Otomanguean branch deep inside Maya territory; their neighbours absorbed them within two centuries.

entries.name: Xochicalco culture
entries.settlement: fortified acropolis trade and ritual centre on a defensible ridge
trade: controlled the central corridor after Teotihuacan fell
entries.beliefs: Feathered Serpent cult pan-Mesoamerican; sky-watching as state religion
entries.fell_by: sacked and burned around 900 CE
entries.notes: A window on the “recovery” centuries: the Feathered Serpent already was everywhere, waiting for the Toltecs to adopt him.
